questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the idiom/phrase. **

Beat around the bush

options.text: To treat a topic, but omit its main points, often intentionally.
Talk bad about a person, often in the absence of that person.
It is wise to ignore hardships and continue with your task.

questions.solution:
Ans: To treat a topic, but omit its main points, often intentionally.

Sol: The phrase ‘beat around the bush’ means to avoid answering a question or to approach something indirectly. Hence, Option 1 is the closest in meaning and is the correct answer. An example sentence is: “The judge told the lawyer to stop beating around the bush and present facts.”

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which will improve the bracketed part of the sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select "no improvement".**

He proposed **(meets)** me at the temple.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**to meet**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**\

 
• **Propose + gerund** means suggest. In this formulation, it has the same meaning as when followed by a that-clause.
 
• **Examples**

 
• *John proposed going to the debate.*
 
• *I propose that we buy a smaller car.*
 
• *I propose buying a smaller car.*

 
• **Propose + infinitive** means intend or offer.
 
• **Examples**

 
• *The Government proposes to bring in new laws.*
 
• *I propose to finish this meeting tomorrow.*
 
• *He proposed to go so I didn't have to.*
 
• *Janet has proposed to take notes and circulate them afterwards.**​​*

Here, 'propose' is used in the sense of offering to meet at the temple, so it should be followed by 'to'.

**The correct sentence is: **‘*He proposed to meet me at the temple*’.

questions.question:
**In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in ****Indirect****/Direct speech.**

"What is your name?" she asked him.

options.text: She asked him what his name is.
She asked him what his name has been.
She asked him what is his name.
She asked him what his name was.

questions.solution:
Ans: She asked him what his name was.

Sol: Sentence 1 uses the incorrect tense (present tense) in the reported speech, Sentence 2 changes the meaning of the sentence by using the past perfect tense and Sentence 3 poses a question in the reported speech, which is grammatically incorrect and not allowed. Only Sentence 4 converts the present tense into past tense and uses correct sentence structure, making it the correct answer.

questions.question:
**In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the idiom/phrase. **

Achilles' heel

options.text: A fatal weakness in spite of overall strength.
A secret weapon to be used as a last resort.
A past deed which one is trying to hide.
The person who is blamed if anything goes wrong.

questions.solution:
Ans: A fatal weakness in spite of overall strength.

Sol: The phrase “Achilles’ heel” means a weakness or vulnerable point in spite of overall strength. Hence, Option 1 is the closest in meaning and is the correct answer. An example sentence is: “Ice cream is my Achilles’ heel in the quest to lose weight.”

questions.question:
**In the following question, a sentence has been given in Active/Passive voice. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Passive/Active voice.**

Varun ate six rotis at dinner.

options.text: At dinner, six rotis was ate by Varun.
At dinner, six rotis were eaten by Varun.
At dinner, Varun had eaten six rotis.
At dinner, had Varun eaten six rotis.

questions.solution:
Ans: At dinner, six rotis were eaten by Varun.

Sol: Sentence 1 uses ‘was’ for a plural noun (rotis), Sentence 3 changes the tense from simple past to past perfect and Sentence 4 completely changes the structure of the sentence and makes it into a conditional. Only Sentence 2 preserves the tense and the meaning and is the correct conversion from Active to Passive voice of the given sentence.

Rebate
questions.solution:

questions.solution:

questions.solution:
Ans: ranging

Sol: Ranging means to vary between specific limits. It fits the sentence appropriately as the sentences defines the limits as anxiety disorders and depression and states that primary care physicians can be trained to detect disease in those limits. Hence, ‘ranging’ is the correct option.

questions.question:

Freedom fighters laboured (1)/ to the good of (2)/the poor enslaved masses.(3)/No Error (4)
questions.solution:
Ans: 2

Sol: The word ‘laboured’ means something done with great difficulty and effort. It is followed by a **‘for’, **and not ‘to’. The phrase ‘for the good of’ means for the benefit of. The correct sentence is: **‘Freedom fighters laboured for the good of the poor enslaved masses.’**
